edges.description: Loss of ACSF3 prevents efficient ATP-dependent activation of malonate and methylmalonate to malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA.
The biochemical disease signature is increased urinary methylmalonic acid and malonic acid.
Malonate accumulation and reduced mitochondrial malonyl-CoA production impair mitochondrial metabolism and mitochondrial protein malonylation.
intermediate_mechanisms: Reduced ACSF3-derived mitochondrial malonyl-CoA and protein malonylation.

edges.description: Reported selected cases include neurologic, psychiatric, and childhood metabolic presentations, but screen-detected cohorts suggest many patients have a favorable or mild course.
Increased methylmalonic acid reports failure to recycle methylmalonate through ACSF3.
Increased malonic acid reports failure to activate malonate through ACSF3.

nodes.description: Biallelic ACSF3 variants reduce mitochondrial malonyl-CoA synthetase / methylmalonyl-CoA synthetase activity. This removes a mitochondrial repair pathway that normally activates malonate and methylmalonate into CoA thioesters.

evidence.snippet: We establish ACSF3 mutations as the cause of CMAMMA and describe the first disease association with a member of the acyl-CoA synthetase (ACS) family, enzymes that activate fatty acids for intermediary metabolism4.

evidence.reference_title: Mammalian ACSF3 protein is a malonyl-CoA synthetase that supplies the chain extender units for mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis.
evidence.snippet: The human candidate protein ACSF3, which has a predicted N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence, was cloned, expressed, and characterized as a 65-kDa acyl-CoA synthetase with extremely high specificity for malonate and methylmalonate.

nodes.description: Reported pathogenic variants include missense, in-frame deletion, and nonsense alleles affecting conserved acyl-CoA synthetase motifs.

evidence.snippet: ACSF3-derived malonyl-CoA was specifically required for lysine malonylation of mitochondrial proteins.
